detail.abstract: Brazil is one of the world's largest agricultural producers, yet the institutional environment that should sustain innovation in the sector operates under persistent uncertainty. Drawing on a closed-door roundtable held in Brasília on 2 September 2026, which brought together Justices of the Superior Court of Justice and the Superior Labour Court, the Minister of Development, Industry, Trade and Services and a Deputy Prosecutor General, this essay identifies legal certainty as the single theme running through every intervention and organises the discussion around four pressure points: judicial revision of technology-licensing contracts; the expected return on private investment; delays in patent examination and regulatory approval; and regulation adopted without impact analysis. A cross-cutting factor is then added: artificial intelligence, which is compressing research cycles and will intensify pressure on all four simultaneously. The analysis combines transaction-cost economics, the law-and-economics account of intellectual property and the author's own theory of contract revision based on risk allocation rather than unforeseeability. The conclusion is that the Brazilian debate has focused on the scope of rights while the demonstrable problem lies in enforcement.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the interaction between output taxation, productivity-enhancing investment, and tax pass-through under Cournot competition. A two-stage n-firm model is developed in which firms first choose cost-reducing investment and subsequently compete in quantities under a specific output tax. Investment reduces marginal production costs and involves a convex investment cost, while firms take the strategic effects of investment on subsequent market competition into account. The model derives the symmetric subgame-perfect equilibrium and characterizes the effects of taxation, investment productivity, and market structure on investment, output, effective marginal cost, and equilibrium prices. The results show that an increase in the output tax reduces both equilibrium output and productivity-enhancing investment. The investment response arises indirectly because taxation reduces the equilibrium production scale and therefore lowers the private return to cost reduction. Lower investment subsequently increases firms' effective marginal production costs. The analysis further shows that greater investment productivity increases both investment and output, while greater competition reduces investment per firm but can increase aggregate industry investment under the maintained parameter conditions. Finally, endogenous investment can amplify tax pass-through and generate tax over-shifting when investment productivity is sufficiently high relative to its cost. These results highlight an investment-mediated channel through which output taxation affects productive efficiency and tax incidence under imperfect competition.

title: Powering Uzbekistan to 2035: Electricity Demand under Growth and Electrification
affiliations: , New Uzbekistan University, Center for Economic Research and Reforms and New Uzbekistan University

detail.title: Powering Uzbekistan to 2035: Electricity Demand under Growth and Electrification
detail.abstract: Rapid economic expansion and a government-led electrification programme are placing Uzbekistan's power system under mounting pressure, yet no transparent, reproducible long-run demand forecast for the country exists in the peer-reviewed literature. This paper fills that gap by coupling the Prophet additive time-series model with a structural trend calibration procedure that converts macroeconomic growth scenarios into annual demand targets through empirically estimated short- and long-run elasticities taken from a companion regional panel study. Hourly load observations from five national control zones (CDC Energiya, 2018–2024) train the model and establish a 2024 national demand anchor of 81.8 TWh. Four scenarios are examined: Business-As-Usual (BAU), an Economic Boom aligned with Uzbekistan's $240 billion GDP target, and two augmented scenarios that add electric vehicle (EV) fleet growth and the electrification of residential space heating under the government's household fuel-switching programme. Under BAU, demand reaches 106.7 TWh by 2030 and 133.8 TWh by 2035; full demand-side electrification under the Boom scenario lifts these figures to 119.7 and 154.2 TWh respectively, an 88.5% cumulative increase over the 2024 baseline. Delta-method propagation of the elasticity standard errors shows that the Boom-BAU gap is precisely identified, whereas the level of the demand path carries a wide confidence corridor dominated by the imprecisely estimated residential price response. Hourly profiling reveals that electrification reshapes the daily load curve into a distinctive double peak — morning heating (06:00–09:00) and evening EV charging (18:00–23:00) — raising peak load to approximately 33,300 MW by 2035 under the upper scenario. These findings point to an urgent need for flexible generation capacity, time-of-use tariffs and demand-response programmes.

detail.abstract: While sustainable credit frameworks are designed to steer capital toward the energy transition, their real-world efficacy depends on how banking regulations handle informational frictions at the counter level. Focusing on small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) credit markets—where physical emissions are high but operational visibility is low—this paper examines the strategic alignment between corporate borrowers, commercial banks, and environmental supervisors. We develop a continuous-type Bayesian game under asymmetric information in which lender screening capacity and supervisory enforcement are endogenously determined. We show that when supervisory reviews reward procedural compliance over physical state verification, commercial lenders face zero marginal return on costly physical monitoring. In equilibrium, banks rationally minimize auditing efforts, prompting borrowing firms—regardless of their true energy efficiency—to adopt green labels. The credit market thus reaches a silent consensus: reported Green Asset Ratios achieve perfection, while physical carbon footprints remain completely stagnant. Moving beyond standard cheap-talk dynamics, we derive explicit analytical thresholds for supervisory penalties and monitoring costs required to break this pooling equilibrium. We outline a pragmatic mechanism design—combining automated administrative energy data, dynamic capital add-ons, and performance-contingent rebates—that bridges the gap between theoretical credit policy and real-world decarbonization.

detail.abstract: National governments increasingly designate cities as flagship sites for climate policy, yet quantitative evaluations of their impact on metropolitan emissions remain limited. This study examines Busan, designated in July 2018 as a flagship pilot under South Korea’s National Strategic Smart City Program. Using a province-year panel from 2010 to 2020, we estimate Busan’s counterfactual emissions intensity via synthetic control with a fifteen-province donor pool, evaluate results through placebo-in-space and in-time tests, and analyze sectoral emissions changes. The synthetic control analysis does not detect a Busan-specific deviation in emissions trajectory compared to similar Korean cities, and both placebo tests support the null. Busan’s modest 6.0% emissions decline post-designation occurred mainly in a volatile sector influenced by national power-sector dynamics, while transport, the largest sector at 40% of emissions, increased by 3.1%, contrary to the overall trend. These findings suggest that climate-relevant designations must be paired with sector-specific policies targeting dominant emissions sources rather than relying on them alone for decarbonization.

detail.title: Energy transition policy and firm supply chain risk: Evidence from China’s new energy vehicle demonstration cities
detail.abstract: Amid the accelerating global energy transition, the supply chain vulnerability of China’s new energy vehicle (NEV) industry, a key carrier of this transition, has become increasingly prominent, and the energy transition policies that drive technological switching and capacity adjustment may themselves trigger supply chain risk. Whether energy transition policy can safeguard supply chain security while advancing green development is therefore central to coordinating high-quality development with economic security. Exploiting China’s NEV Demonstration City policy as a quasi-natural experiment, and using an unbalanced panel of 875 Chinese A-share listed firms along the NEV industry chain over 2008–2024, we employ a difference-in-differences approach to identify the causal effect of energy transition policy on firm supply chain risk, which we measure with a bullwhip-effect index. We find that the policy significantly reduces NEV firms’ supply chain risk, a conclusion that survives PSM-DID estimation, placebo tests, and a battery of robustness checks. Mechanism analyses show that the policy curbs risk by stimulating technological innovation, easing financing constraints, and improving firms’ supply chain position, and that government subsidies and analyst coverage significantly amplify these effects. Heterogeneity analyses point to a size-threshold pattern: the effect is significant for large firms but not for small ones, and it holds for both state-owned and non-state-owned firms without significant ownership differentiation. By incorporating supply chain risk into the evaluation framework of energy transition policy, this study provides micro-level causal evidence and policy guidance for the coordinated advancement of green development and industrial chain security.

detail.abstract: Cross-institutional collaboration in credit risk modeling offers considerable potential to enhance predictive performance and foster financial stability, but it is frequently constrained by privacy concerns and regulatory barriers. This paper presents a practical framework for privacy-preserving inter-bank logistic regression based on secret sharing within a Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) setting. detail.abstract: The demand for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) has increased across Europe, but at very different rates. Most existing studies focus on single countries, making it challenging to compare preferences and identify why adoption differs. In this paper, we compare preferences for BEVs and PHEVs across six European markets with highly varying adoption levels: the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, Italy, and Spain.We estimate mixed logit models with country-specific effects using stated preference data from a harmonised European survey with approx. 1,000 respondents per country. The models are used to calculate willingness-to-pay measures for vehicle attributes and quantify preferences for fuel types across population segments. We observe large differences in preferences depending on access to home charging across countries, with the gap particularly pronounced in Germany. Preferences related to both BEVs and PHEVs are most negative in the Czech Republic, and most positive in Denmark, Italy, and Spain. For Germany, the relative ranking is dependent on access to home charging. These results indicate that countries face different barriers to electric vehicle adoption. In some cases, improving charging access and economic incentives may be sufficient, while in others, barriers related to attitudes and awareness may require targeted measures beyond infrastructure and pricing.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how an exogenous path of private learning is translated, through strategic trading and competitive filtering, into an endogenous path of public price discovery. I separate the evolution of the true fundamental, the insider's gradual learning, and the market maker's learning through order flow. In discrete time, equilibrium is characterized by a deterministic recurrence, with a viability threshold and transversality condition selecting the unique infinitehorizon path. In the continuous-time limit, the equilibrium admits an almost closed-form geometric characterization: after a hazard-dependent change of clock, public learning is given by the pinned greatest convex minorant of transformed private learning. Contact corresponds to informational catch-up, while noncontact represents private information carried forward and revealed only gradually. The framework accommodates finite-time, asymptotic, and repeated episodes of catch-up and separation. More broadly, information-processing technologies can reshape the time profile of private learning in different ways. A sufficiently front-loaded burst of private learning can generate a persistent lag in price discovery, with the market catching up only asymptotically.

detail.abstract: I study whether the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Medicaid expansion changed allcause mortality in Illinois and the five states that border it. I build a county-year panel of age-standardised mortality rates for 599 counties from 2011 to 2019 and compare counties in the four states that expanded Medicaid (Illinois, Iowa and Kentucky in January 2014; Indiana in February 2015) with counties in the two states that did not (Missouri and Wisconsin), using a two-way fixed effects difference-indifferences design. The estimates show mortality rising by about 10.2 deaths per 100,000 (1.1 percent) in expansion counties relative to non-expansion counties, with a larger gap in rural counties. I do not read this as evidence that Medicaid expansion raised mortality. The relative increase comes entirely from Iowa, Kentucky and Indiana; Illinois itself shows no change. Pre-expansion trends are not cleanly parallel, allowing state-specific linear trends halves the estimate, and with six state clusters the wild-cluster-bootstrap p-values range from 0.04 to 0.11. The two obvious confounders do not explain it either: drug-induced deaths rose in all six states and a difference-indifferences on state drug-death rates is zero, and the timing of cuts to food assistance (SNAP) through reinstated time limits runs the wrong way across states to explain it. A dose-response test shows a weak, fragile gradient in county coverage gains. What remains is a divergence in nondrug mortality between three expansion states and their neighbours that this design cannot attribute to the policy. The main lesson is methodological: a six-state design with all-cause mortality as the outcome cannot separate the effect of Medicaid expansion from regional shocks that hit the same states at the same time.
